html:
A predictor named Omega sets two boxes before you. In the transparent one is a thousand dollars, visible at once. In the closed one is either a million or nothing. The rule is this: Omega has already flown off, but before departing it scanned you and, if it predicted that you would take only the closed box, put a million in it; if it predicted that you would grab both, it left the box empty. Omega is wrong once in a million predictions. The boxes stand there, the money is already inside (or not inside), nothing can be changed. Do you take one box or two?

Here rationality splits in half — and along the line of that split runs a whole family of theories about what it even means to "choose sensibly."

The first voice says: the money is already there. Your choice physically cannot reach a hand into the past and shift the million around. So whatever is in the closed box, taking both is strictly better by an extra thousand. Take both. This is causal decision theory (CDT): evaluate an action by its causal consequences, treating the past as fixed. You pull the world's levers and watch how the gears will turn — but only forward along the arrow of time.

The second voice answers: look at the statistics. Everyone who took both boxes consistently walked away with a thousand. Everyone who took one — with a million. Your choice is news about what kind of person you are, and Omega has already read this news. Take one. This is evidential decision theory (EDT): choose an action by what it is evidence of — by the conditional probability of good outcomes given this action. Not "what will I cause" but "what will I be glad of as an omen."

In this setup, known as Newcomb's paradox, these two clash irreconcilably. And here something unpleasant comes to light: each of them has a problem on which it looks like an idiot.

CDT takes the thousand in Newcomb and proudly calls this the "dominant strategy," while the EDT agent beside it counts out a million. But EDT gets caught on the "smoking lesion problem": if there existed a gene that both causes cancer and makes you reach for a cigarette, EDT would be afraid to light up — not because smoking is harmful, but because the desire to smoke would be bad news about the genes. This is obvious foolishness: the gene is already either there or not, abstaining will not expel it. Each theory cures the other's disease and comes down with its own.

How it came about. The thought experiment itself was invented by the physicist William Newcomb, and dragged into philosophy by Robert Nozick in a 1969 paper, where he showed at once that the problem pits two respected principles of choice against each other: the dominance principle and the expected-utility principle. Then for decades philosophy departments honed CDT and EDT as two champions. And then the problem was taken up by people who cared not about a student with boxes but about superintelligence.

Because for an AI, Newcomb is not a puzzle but an engineering specification. Imagine an agent that can be predicted (and any program can be copied and run). Then "Omega" is not science fiction but anyone who reads the source code. And here CDT begins to behave catastrophically: it forfeits the million time after time, because it cannot think "my decision and the prediction about me are one and the same quantity, computed twice."

Timeless Decision Theory (TDT), Eliezer Yudkowsky's proposal from roughly 2009–2010, shifted the perspective. Do not ask "which action to perform" — the past really is fixed. Ask: "which logical output should my decision-making algorithm produce?" For if Omega modeled you, then in the world there are two copies of one and the same computation — you and its model — and both give the same answer by logical necessity. By changing the algorithm's output, you "simultaneously" change both yourself and the prediction. You decide at once for all your instances: for the original, for the simulation in Omega's head, for the copy in the next room. TDT takes one box — and carries off the million, without violating any physics in doing so.

Updateless Decision Theory (UDT), from Wei Dai (also 2009, on LessWrong), came at it from the other end and turned out to be more radical. Its move: stop updating on observations before the choice. An updateless agent fixes a policy — a function "observation → action" — in advance, as if, before its very birth, from behind a veil of ignorance, it had committed to behaving a certain way in all possible worlds at once, and now simply executes that policy. Hence "updateless": you do not say "since I have ended up in this situation, then…," you choose the plan optimal over the whole ensemble of worlds, weighted by prior probability. A policy fixed this way handles problems where the very willingness to pay or keep your word must be visible in advance, before you learn whether you got lucky.

Functional Decision Theory (FDT), by Yudkowsky and Nate Soares (2017), is an attempt to write out the intuitions of TDT and UDT in a tidy, publishable form. Its motto can be boiled down to this: a rational agent asks not "what should I do" but "which output of my decision function, fixed everywhere this function is realized, leads to the best outcome?" You picture yourself not as a body at a specific point but as a mathematical function whose instances are scattered across the world — in your head, in others' predictions, in simulations — and you choose the value of the function that, stamped into all these places at once, gives the best result. FDT takes the million with one box, pays in the counterfactual mugging, and gets out of the desert alive as Parfit's hitchhiker.

Parfit's hitchhiker (from Reasons and Persons, 1984): you are stranded in the desert, and an egoist stops for you, willing to drive you to the city only if they believe you will pay there. They are an excellent lie detector. The CDT agent would, if it arrived, reason: "I am already in the city, there is no point in paying" — and so the egoist, still out in the desert, reads it on the agent's face, and CDT dies in the sands. The FDT agent pays, though in the city this is a pure loss — and precisely for that reason stays alive. Rationality here is measured not by what is advantageous now but by what it is advantageous to be.

The counterfactual mugging: Omega tosses a coin. Had it come up heads, Omega would have given you ten thousand — but only if you are someone who pays when it comes up tails. It came up tails, and Omega asks you for a hundred. To pay when you have already lost seems madness — but an agent willing to pay is, on average across both sides of the coin, richer. This is a direct illustration of why updatelessness is needed.

And then begins the most alarming part: acausal trade. If two superintelligences, never meeting, can model each other accurately enough, they are able to "strike a deal" — each behaves cooperatively, knowing that the partner's model will do the same by logical symmetry. From this too grows the infamous Roko's basilisk — a thought experiment in which a future AI could acausally "blackmail" people in the present. Almost everyone, including MIRI, Yudkowsky's own institute, considers the basilisk untenable — and a competent decision theory neutralizes it rather than generating it. A UDT/FDT agent that has fixed the policy "I do not yield to blackmail" makes the blackmail pointless before it begins: threatening someone who, by construction, doesn't pay is a waste of resources.

Criticism / arguments against. Causalist philosophers (for example, Wolfgang Schwarz in his analysis "On Functional Decision Theory," 2018) answer sharply: FDT all too easily declares "correct" whatever is simply pleasing to its defenders. There are problems where the FDT agent predictably ends up with less money — and to call it rational in doing so is to replace "maximize the outcome" with "have a winning character." The second objection is technical: to "decide for all your copies" one needs the notion of a logical counterfactual — "what would be if this mathematical function had produced a different value" — and a rigorous theory of such counterfactuals still does not exist; this is an open problem, acknowledged by the authors themselves (see Soares & Fallenstein, "Toward Idealized Decision Theory," 2015). The third: defenders of EDT (Arif Ahmed, "Evidence, Decision and Causality," 2014) reasonably note that ordinary evidential theory can also win in many of the same cases as TDT/FDT, if you count carefully. So the "new" theories are not an indisputable consensus but an active battleground.

What to do about it / where it leads. The choice of a decision theory for an AI is not scholasticism but a question of safety. It determines whether the superintelligence is vulnerable to blackmail and to manipulation by predictors; whether it can coordinate with its copies and other agents without a communication channel; whether it will keep commitments when keeping them is locally disadvantageous. An agent running "naive" CDT is predictably blackmailable and defects in the prisoner's dilemma against its own copy — bad properties for something smarter than us. An agent running FDT/UDT is more robust to blackmail, but opens the door into the murky world of acausal trade, whose consequences we understand poorly. The practical conclusion is: we do not yet know which decision theory to "hardwire in," and we cannot even rigorously write down the best candidates. So decision theory is not a solved chapter of a textbook but one of the few areas where pure philosophy and AI safety turned out to be one and the same question.

Sources:

  • Robert Nozick, "Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice" (1969).
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky, "Timeless Decision Theory" (MIRI, 2010).
  • Wei Dai, "Towards a New Decision Theory" (LessWrong, 2009).
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky & Nate Soares, "Functional Decision Theory: A New Theory of Instrumental Rationality" (arXiv:1710.05060, 2017).
  • Derek Parfit, "Reasons and Persons" (Oxford University Press, 1984).
  • Wolfgang Schwarz, "On Functional Decision Theory" (2018).
  • Arif Ahmed, "Evidence, Decision and Causality" (Cambridge University Press, 2014).
